summary:
La Guajira stands under the national framework of Colombia, which is among the most developed in Latin America and is what a trans visitor in this frontier department meets directly. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016, adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

The source inventory identifies no La Guajira-specific legal, document, entry, screening, facilities or care finding that departs from that national position, and no enforcement deviation material enough to score separately; the department is assessed at the national score.

What distinguishes La Guajira is who controls conduct on the ground. The department sits in the country's frontier belt where "orden público" regimes mean armed groups rather than departmental police effectively regulate conduct. In March 2024 armed groups in Guajira posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans".

A 2025 report by Caribe Afirmativo documents the territorial expansion of violence and the insufficiency of the state response, with trans women displaced from such departments because of their gender identity by the same armed actors that displace others. National context reaching this department: the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025, and one count recorded 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025 alone.

Targeted violence continues in ordinary urban settings as well. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in Bello, Antioquia, near Medellín in April 2025; a video of the assault went viral from 5 April showing her with fractured limbs in a creek unable to swim, before she drowned. Her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was". President Petro ordered an urgent investigation and solidarity events were held in several cities.

The courts have also intervened directly in detention: a Colombian court ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.
tangentialFactors:
Armed-group "social cleansing" campaigns against LGBT people are documented elsewhere in Colombia as the pattern La Guajira sits inside. In Caquetá department, flyers on the street and via WhatsApp named "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets. A trans woman and local election candidate was told by three armed men she had one week to leave town, hid for a week, then fled at night; a second trans woman said a friend was killed. Eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024 and 41 in 2023, and discrimination limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work. In that department a trans salon owner, Tatiana Cespedes, was forced to relocate twice after death threats, and a friend of the trans woman Yesenia Rodríguez was killed.

Reporting of 6 August 2025 by CNN's 'As Equals' project found that the viral Millerey video shocked the country but that killings continued under armed gangs, framing being queer in parts of the country as "to sign your own death sentence".

International scrutiny is active. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected and that widespread discrimination and violence must be addressed urgently as killings rise. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.

Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity.

Public opinion is a live variable. Colombian society is described as generally conservative on LGBT issues, and an October 2019 Invamer poll reached 50% support for same-sex marriage for the first time, with 47% opposed.
localsOnly:
Consensual same-sex activity has been legal in Colombia since 1981, and Congress passed a law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation in 2011.

The right to change legal gender has existed since 1993, and since 2015 gender change has been possible without psychiatric or physical evaluations. Constitutional Court jurisprudence recognises recognition on the basis of self-recognition, with no surgical requirement.

Same-sex couples have been able to marry since April 2016, making Colombia the fourth Latin American country to do so, and were granted full adoption rights in 2015. Transgender people have been allowed to serve openly in the military since 2015.

National identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025, and a comprehensive trans law remained under legislative consideration in 2025.

Prison conditions are governed by court order: a Colombian court has ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the national and departmental homicide counts cited for Colombia include killings recorded specifically within La Guajira is unresolved; the inventory supplies no departmental disaggregation, and no La Guajira-specific killing of a trans person is named in the sources.

Whether the 2011 anti-discrimination statute, the notary-based gender-marker route and the court's detention ruling are applied with equal accessibility in La Guajira's rural and municipal jurisdictions is not sourced either way.

No source addresses access to trans-specific healthcare, hormone treatment, shelter or safe facilities within La Guajira, and none addresses whether a visitor's foreign documents carrying a trans or non-binary marker are accepted locally; these remain not sourced rather than absent.

The dedicated English-language entry on the La Guajira department itself yielded no usable finding on LGBT or trans rights, so all departmental content here derives from national reporting and from reports on the frontier-violence pattern.
